## Abstract

Although therapeutic B cell depletion dramatically resolves inflammation in many diseases in which antibodies appear not to play a central role, distinct extrafollicular pathogenic B cell subsets that accumulate in disease lesions have hitherto not been identified. The circulating immunoglobulin D (IgD)−CD27−CXCR5−CD11c+ DN2 B cell subset has been previously studied in some autoimmune diseases. A distinct IgD−CD27−CXCR5−CD11c− DN3 B cell subset accumulates in the blood both in IgG4-related disease, an autoimmune disease in which inflammation and fibrosis can be reversed by B cell depletion, and in severe COVID-19. These DN3 B cells prominently accumulate in the end organs of IgG4-related disease and in lung lesions in COVID-19, and double-negative B cells prominently cluster with CD4+ T cells in these lesions. Extrafollicular DN3 B cells may participate in tissue inflammation and fibrosis in autoimmune fibrotic diseases, as well as in COVID-19.

## Abstract

## Abstract

Allard-Chamard and Kaneko et al. show that extrafollicular B cell subsets, including DN3 B cells, preferentially infiltrate end organs, where they physically interact with CD4+ T cells. Since many inflammatory diseases respond to B cell depletion, specific extrafollicular B cell subsets, including DN3 B cells, could represent more specific future targets for therapeutic intervention.

## Introduction

T-B interactions that occur in secondary lymphoid organs in the context of antigen overload and/or dysregulated inflammation may favor extrafollicular over germinal center-type responses.1 , 2 Extrafollicular B cell populations that are generated in a disease-specific manner may potentially contribute to disease progression and disease sequelae. We and others have revealed the presence of subsets of antigen-specific disease-related immunoglobulin D (IgD)−CD27− double-negative (DN) B cells that accumulate in the blood of COVID-19 patients including those with severe disease.2 , 3

While many studies have focused on extrafollicular responses in the context of autoantibody generation, there are inflammatory diseases that respond to B cell depletion in which autoantibodies may not play a central role. It is therefore relevant to pay close attention to extrafollicular B cell responses in the context of organ damage since extrafollicular B cell subsets that are largely seen only in the context of disease might accumulate in tissues and contribute to tissue inflammation and fibrosis beyond their potential contributions to extrafollicular antibody generation.

IgG4-related disease (IgG4-RD) is a systemic disease that responds extremely well clinically to B cell depletion,4 , 5 and the improvement extends, surprisingly, even to the reversal of tissue fibrosis.6 The indolent nature of this autoimmune fibrotic disease facilitates a more ready response to therapies compared with systemic sclerosis, for instance, and makes it a particularly useful disorder in which to examine the adaptive immune onset of fibrosis.7 We have also shown that extrafollicular B cell activation is prominent in IgG4-RD since isotype switching to IgG4 is driven by interleukin-4 (IL-4; and IL-10)-expressing T helper cells (pre-GC T follicular helper cells) outside germinal centers.8 , 9

Lung fibrosis similar to what was observed after severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS) and Middle Eastern respiratory syndrome (MERS)10 , 11 , 12 has been seen on a much broader demographic scale in COVID-19.13 , 14 , 15 Fibrosis ranges from small lesions that persist in patients to the very extensive fibrosis that severely compromises lung function in COVID-19 and can require lung transplantation.16 From a mechanistic standpoint, macrophage activation by SARS coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) in COVID-19 has been shown to generate a profibrotic macrophage phenotype reminiscent of that seen in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF).17 So far, few, if any, studies have analyzed infiltrating B lymphocyte subsets in the lung in severe COVID-19, and none have simultaneously interrogated draining lymph nodes.

We compared DN B cell subsets in blood and inflamed tissues in COVID-19 with those in IgG4-RD, a disease in which B cells are causally implicated in tissue inflammation and fibrosis. We show that these B cell subsets are generated in draining lymph nodes in COVID-19 and that while both antigen-specific DN2 and DN3 B cells expand in the blood in both these conditions, DN3 B cells, but not DN2 B cells, make up a large proportion of disease-infiltrating B cells in COVID-19 lungs as well as in the fibrotic end organs in IgG4-RD. DN3 B cells might potentially contribute to the initiation of fibrosis in both IgG4-RD and in COVID-19 and should be investigated as possible drivers of persistent inflammation and fibrosis in the post-acute sequelae of COVID-19.

## Results

### Distinct populations of B cells, including DN B cells, emerge in the blood in IgG4-RD and COVID-19

Because of our concerns about inflammation leading to fibrosis in COVID-19 and the potential for B cells to have a detrimental role in this disease, we chose to compare B cell populations in IgG4-RD, a multisystem fibro-inflammatory disease in which B cell depletion is extremely effective, and in COVID-19, examining both the blood and affected end organs. In our previous studies on IgG4-RD, we had shown that plasmablasts are abundant and expand in the blood5 and that disease tissues contain what we described as plasmablasts based on staining for cells that express CD19 but not CD20.18 We recognized that our previous studies may have missed many activated B cells and that it was possible that other B cell subsets might be more prominent in disease tissues than plasmablasts. The purpose of our initial studies on the blood was to identify the range of activated B cells in the blood in these diseases in order to inform our subsequent tissue analyses. ### DN3 B cells have a distinctive signature distinct from DN2 B cells

The overall phenotypes of disease-related B cell populations are likely influenced by the milieus in which they are generated, and transcriptomic analyses of DN1and DN2 populations in IgG4-RD broadly resembled the transcriptomes of DN1 and DN2 B cells described in lupus24 (Figures 4A, 4B, and S2A). In contrast, DN3 B cells exhibited a unique signature with a strong signature of proliferation and the unfolded protein response (Figure 4C). They exhibit some features of plasmablasts and antibody-producing cells while also expressing high levels of RNA-encoding IgG4 (Figures 4D and S2A). They also, like DN2 B cells, expressed a number of genes characteristic of cytotoxic CD8+ T cells, cytotoxic CD4+ T cells, and natural killer (NK) cells (Figures S2A and S2B). Both DN2 and DN3 B cells expressed SLAMF7 at the RNA and protein levels (Figures S2A and S2B). The expression of SLAMF7 in DN2 B cells has also been described in transcriptomic studies on patients with lupus.23 Perforin expression in DN3 B cells was, however, generally low (Figure S2A). All subsets expressed discernible HLA class II, but plasmablasts expressed lower HLA class II levels than DN3 B cells. As was seen in COVID-19, all DN B cell subsets infiltrated the inflamed end organ, and they could theoretically contribute to fibrosis, especially since B cell depletion has a profound histological and therapeutic benefit.

DN B cells probably contribute to the fibrotic changes in IgG4-RD (given the dramatic improvement seen with B cell depletion therapy) and potentially to the fibrotic sequelae of COVID-19, possibly by interacting with CD4+ T cells and reactivating them in the tissue setting via antigen presentation (and possibly also the release of cytokines). To qualitatively ask if true T-B conjugates were generated in the end organs in both IgG4-RD and COVID-19, we used the same approach used in Figure 3 that computationally detects cytoplasmic overlap between cells and showed the presence of true T-B conjugates in COVID-19 and IgG4-RD (Figure S4). To establish that cells in the infiltrates included IgD−CD27− DN B cells (and since we had confirmed that DN2 and DN3 B cells express SLAMF7; Figure S2), we stained tissues with CD19, IgD, CD27, and SLAMF7. As seen in Figure S4C, activated DN2/3 B cells interact with CD4+ T cells. As DN2 B cells are relatively infrequent in tissues, most of these T-B interactions are likely with DN3 B cells, suggesting that this subset of activated B cells (and potentially interactions of CD4+ T cells with plasmablasts as well) may be drivers of pathology.

## Discussion

Why is B cell depletion so effective in an inflammatory, fibrotic disease in which autoantibodies do not have an established pathogenic role? Are there disease-specific extrafollicular B cells that infiltrate tissues that could be potential drivers of inflammation and fibrosis upstream of the activation of myeloid cells, fibroblasts, and myofibroblasts?

The present studies establish that IgD−CD27− DN B cells, especially DN3 B cells, generated in a disease context are abundant in lymph nodes, infiltrate inflamed tissues, and could be important drivers of inflammation and fibrosis. While DN2 B cells have been described as a potential source of autoantibodies in lupus23 and are relatively enriched among circulating B cells in COVID-19 patients,2 , 3 we show here that they are not abundant in COVID-19 lymph nodes and are relatively sparse in both IgG4-RD and COVID-19 end organs. DN3 B cells, however, may be of pathogenic relevance in IgG4-RD, an inflammatory fibrotic disorder in which B cell depletion dramatically attenuates disease, as well as in COVID-19. In COVID-19, B cell depletion clearly does not have a role in management. However, a detailed understanding of the biology of DN3 B cells could eventually lead to better targeted therapies for IgG4-RD and other fibrotic diseases including COVID-19. They may also contribute to autoimmunity since DN2 and DN3 B cells have been shown to correlate with levels of autoantibodies in severe COVID-19 infection.25

Tissue-infiltrating extrafollicular DN3 B cells arise in the context of immune dysregulation in both IgG4-RD and COVID-19. It may be assumed that the massive inflammatory immune response that occurs as a result of the attenuation of the anti-viral state by SARS-CoV-2 results in a lymph node cytokine milieu that contributes to the dysfunctional regulatory T cells described in COVID-1926; this may be a factor both in the loss of tolerance and the generation of DN B cells in severe disease. Although the exact ontology of DN B cells is yet to be defined, they most likely reflect B cells that differentiate following extrafollicular T collaboration. As proposed by Jenks et al.,23 the B cell receptor (BCR) repertoire of DN2 B cells is connected to the repertoire of activated naive B cells and plasma cells. Nonetheless, the exact ontology of most DN B cell subsets is still unclear. In the late-stage fibrotic lungs of patients with COVID-19, innate immune cells dominate.16 , 17 No previous studies have examined B cell populations in the lung parenchyma in COVID-19. However, as in IgG4-RD,27 activated CD4+ T cells, especially cytotoxic CD4+ T cells, are prominent both in the blood and end organs in COVID-19.28 , 29 It remains to be determined whether DN3 B cells collaborate with activated CD4+ T cells in the pathogenesis of IgG4-RD or in the pulmonary sequelae of COVID-19.

Given that many immune-mediated fibrotic diseases have dramatically improved after anti-CD20-mediated B cell deletion, it is reasonable to assume that during convalescence following COVID-19, activated B cell subsets have the capacity to either secrete profibrotic molecules or to collaborate with CD4+ T cells to drive fibrosis and that in some patients with COVID-19, these B cells may be contributors to fibrotic changes in the lungs and other tissues and may thus be responsible for some of unwanted sequelae of COVID-19 infection. The known fibrotic sequelae of COVID-19 might be either driven by T and B cells that recognize persistent SARS-CoV-2 antigens or possibly by autoreactive T and B cells that have been generated as a result of a broad break in immunological tolerance, followed by the infiltration of end organs by activated T and B cell subsets that collaborate to drive fibrotic sequelae not unlike those that might occur in IgG4-RD and systemic sclerosis.

In conclusion, our studies indicate that the extrafollicular B cell response that is readily induced in the altered, inflammatory milieu created in draining lymph nodes in certain diseases generates disease-related B cell populations. We show that a specific extrafollicular B cell population, DN3 B cells, generated in COVID-19 and in IgG4-RD, both diseases characterized by tissue inflammation and fibrosis, infiltrate tissues. These data suggest that DN3 B cells should be further investigated as potential drivers of fibrosis both in IgG4-RD and in COVID-19.

### Limitations of the study

There are a few limitations of the study. The peripheral blood studies on IgG4-RD were designed to explore the relative proportions of different activated B cell subsets, and the healthy controls were not matched in terms of demographics. Among the small number of disease controls, the small number of patients with lupus had active disease, but disease scores were not calculated. In our tissue studies, we have not yet performed deep characterization of T-B conjugates in terms of additional B and T cell markers and HLA class II expression on DN3 B cells and plasma cells in tissues.

### Method details

#### Multi-color immunofluorescence staining

Tissue samples were fixed in formalin, embedded in paraffin, and sectioned. These specimens were incubated with the following antibodies: anti-CD4 (clone: CM153A; Biocare Medical), anti-CD19 (clone: SKU310; Biocare Medical), anti-CD20 (clone: LN26; Novus Biological), anti-Bcl6 (clone: LN22; Biocare Medical), anti-IgD (clone: AA093; DAKO), anti-CD27 (clone: ab131254; Abcam), anti-IgG (clone: ab109489; Abcam), anti-SLAMF7 (clone: HPA055945; Sigma-Aldrich) and anti-CD11c (clone: ab52632; Abcam) followed by incubation with a secondary antibody using an Opal™ Multiplex Kit (Perkin Elmer). The samples were mounted with ProLong™ Diamond Antifade mountant containing DAPI (Invitrogen).

#### Microscopy and quantitative image analysis

Images of the tissue specimens were acquired using the TissueFAXS platform (TissueGnostics). For quantitative analysis, the entire area of the tissue was acquired as a digital grayscale image in five channels with filter settings for FITC, Cy3, Cy5 and AF75 in addition to DAPI. Cells of a given phenotype were identified and quantitated using the TissueQuest software (TissueGnostics), with cut-off values determined relative to the positive controls. This microscopy-based multicolor tissue cytometry software permits multicolor analysis of single cells within tissue sections similar to flow cytometry. StrataQuest (TissueGnostics) software was also used to quantify cell-to-cell contact. In the StrataQuest cell-to-cell contact application, masks of the nuclei based on DAPI staining establish the inner boundary of the cytoplasm and the software “looks” outwards toward the plasma membrane boundary. The software looks for overlap of 2 cells in a 3-pixel distance from the nucleus boundary. If in this 3-pixel wide ring area, any pixel intersection of the 2 cells is required to establish a ‘‘contact’’ criterion. Although the software has been developed and validated more recently, the principle of the method and the algorithms used have been described in detail elsewhere.30

#### Flow cytometry and DN B cell sorting

For DN sorting, 30 million fresh PBMCs were stained within 2 h of isolation. Prior to antibody staining, Fc receptors were blocked using human TruStain FcX (422302; BioLegend) at room temperature for 10 min. Cells were surface stained in two steps for 30 min each. Initially, CXCR5 staining was performed at 37C as the clone J252D4 highly depends on its target protein’s 3D conformation; the rest of the staining was performed at 4C. All staining was conducted, protected from light, using optimized concentrations of fluorochrome-conjugated primary antibodies for 30 min in the presence of 50 μL of Brilliant Stain Buffer (BD Biosciences) to minimize the interaction of polymeric dyes and improve discrete fluorochrome readout. SYTOX AADvanced Dead Cell Stain (S10274; Thermo Fisher Scientific) was added as well immediately before performing sorting to exclude dead cell. The B cell panel (clone, manufacturer) was composed of: CD3 (UCHT1, BD Biosciences), CD19 (SJ25C1, BioLegend), CD27 (L128, BD Biosciences), IgD (IA6-2, BD Biosciences), CD38 (HB-7, BioLegend), CD20 (2H7, BD Biosciences), IgG (G18-145, BD Biosciences), IgM (G20-127, BD Biosciences), IgA (IS11-8E10, Miltenyi), FcRL4 (413D12, Biolegend), SLAMF7 (235614, BD Biosciences), CD11c (Bu15, BioLegend), and CXCR5 (J252D4, BioLegend). For analysis on the cytometer, the same panel was used however the vital stain was switched for the live/dead fixable blue stain (Thermo Fisher) at a concentration of 1:1000 for 30 min in PBS and cells fixed using 4% paraformaldehyde for 30 min at 4C prior to analysis. Sorting was performed on a Special Order Research Products Aria II (BD Biosciences). Rainbow tracking beads (8 peaks calibration beads, Fisher) were used to ensure consistent signals between flow cytometry batches. Compensation was performed using VersaComp Antibody Capture Beads (Beckman Coulter). Cells were collected in RLT Plus buffer supplemented in β-mercaptoethanol according to manufacturer instruction to preserve RNA (Qiagen) and stored at −80C until used. Flow cytometry was performed on a BD Symphony (BD Biosciences, San Jose, CA). FCS files were analyzed, and B cell subsets were quantified using FlowJo software (version 10). Flow cytometry of COVID-19 samples were performed as previously described.3 Antibodies used are detailed in Table S3.

#### RNA-seq

Total RNA, from cells harvested in RLT Plus/β-mercaptoethanol buffer, was isolated using the RNeasy plus Micro Kit (Qiagen) and RNA-seq libraries were subsequently prepared following the SMART-Seq2 protocol.31 Sequencing was performed on a NextSeq 500 instrument (Illumina) with 35–base pair paired-end sequencing. A dept of about 10 million reads was obtained from each sample and reads were analyzed as detailed below. The data generated were deposited in the National Center for Biotechnology Information’s Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) and can be accessed with the GEO series accession # GSE220582.

#### Computational RNA-seq pipelines

RNA-seq was performed using the pipelines we previously described.32 In short, we aligned our raw reads to the University of California, Santa Cruz hg38 reference transcriptome followed by transcript quantification and normalization using RSEM v1.25.0. We used Refseq for gene annotations. Differentially expressed genes were identified using empirical Bayes hierarchical modeling using the R package EBSeq package and Homer’s findGO.pl module was then used to perform functional enrichment.

### Quantification and statistical analysis

GraphPad Prism version 9.0 was used for all statistical analysis and linear regression performed on tissue studies, flow cytometry and clinical correlations. Two-tailed Mann-Whitney U test was used to calculate p values for continuous, non-parametric variables. For comparing more than one population, Kruskal-Wallis testing was used with Dunn’s multiple comparison testing. Correlations were assessed using Spearman rank correlation. Univariate and multivariate logistic regression models were developed. The Maximum likelihood method was used to estimate model parameters, and significance was tested using the Wald test statistic. Logistic regression was performed using the R package version 3.6.0 and SAS software version 9.4 (SAS Institute, Cary, North Carolina). All p-values are two-sided and were not corrected for multiple comparisons. A p value of < 0.05 was considered significant.
